frontMatter.title: The Scoreboard: All 65 Languages Ranked
frontMatter.description: Every score in the 65-language comparison in one place — the ranked table, the six Core, eight Ecosystem, and six Readiness dimension sub-scores, and the complete per-language mechanism data behind each number.

frontMatterLines: description: Every score in the 65-language comparison in one place — the ranked table, the six Core, eight Ecosystem, and six Readiness dimension sub-scores, and the complete per-language mechanism data behind each number.

blocks.q: **Companion to:** [The Great Language Smackdown](index.qmd) · [the Criteria](scoring-criteria.qmd) · [the Scoring Model](objective-coupling-scoring-model.qmd)

blocks.p: This page holds every number in the comparison. Every table responds to the controls above it: type to filter, and choose a key to re-rank. The first table ranks all 65 languages by the **ranking score** — coupling, lifted by at most 15% for readiness — with the star band that follows from Core coupling, and shows Ecosystem coupling alongside. The next three give the per-dimension sub-scores that produce those totals. The last table gives the mechanism-presence data behind every score, so any number can be reproduced from first principles. The criteria are on [the Criteria](scoring-criteria.qmd); the arithmetic, the presence rules, and the ranking rule are on [the Scoring Model](objective-coupling-scoring-model.qmd).

*Higher is better for the score column. The leading (score) column is a score; every (cost) column is a cost, where 0 means no mechanism is charged. Analysis date: June 2026. The 'Platform' column is the language's platform/domain coupling.*

**The leading column is a score; the rest are costs.** A dimension carries a cost, not a percentage: `0` means the language forces no mechanism in that dimension, and a negative number is the cost it forces. The subtotal is capped at −15, which is what the total uses; where the cap bites, the uncapped cost follows in parentheses, so two languages pinned at the cap stay distinguishable. The cells therefore do not sum to the total.

High score = Standardized tooling, rich ecosystem decouples from platform
Low score = Fragmented build systems, limited libraries couple to toolchain
High score = Backward compatible, stable, no breaking changes
Low score = Frequent breaking changes couple codebase to specific versions
High score = Works well across multiple domains
Low score = Couples to specific domains; general-purpose work costs more
High score = Gentle, quick to productivity
Low score = Steep, productivity couples to deep expertise
High score = Concise, readable, minimal boilerplate
Low score = Verbose, boilerplate couples intent to ceremony
High score = Excellent tools, easy to test/debug
Low score = Poor tools couple understanding to manual inspection
High score = Memory safe, type safe, prevents vulnerabilities
Low score = Unsafe, couples correctness to security awareness

blocks.p: How each language builds reproducibly, ships verifiably, can be observed, is quick to work in, connects to other languages, and is governed. Higher is better; the score is reported separately from the two coupling scores.

**The leading column is a score; the rest are costs.** A dimension carries a cost, not a percentage: `0` means the language forces no mechanism in that dimension, and a negative number is the cost it forces. The subtotal is capped at −15, which is what the total uses; where the cap bites, the uncapped cost follows in parentheses, so two languages pinned at the cap stay distinguishable. The cells therefore do not sum to the total.
